When Machines Speak, Matter Is Revealing Physics
Dr. Moh Kolbehdari
text:

When Machines Speak, Matter Is Revealing Physics​We often call the sounds of machines noise.

A train sings as it accelerates.
A transformer hums.
A GPU whines.
An induction cooker changes pitch.
An MRI scanner knocks and roars.

But these sounds are not meaningless.

They are the audible result of energy moving through matter.

Much of the physical world we experience directly is shaped by electromagnetism. Atoms form chemical bonds through electromagnetic interaction. Materials gain stiffness, structure, conductivity, and mechanical response through those same interactions. Human bodies, machines, circuit boards, motors, coils, housings, and transformers are all built from this organized matter.

When electrical energy enters a machine, it rarely stays in only one form.

It may become a magnetic field.
That field may produce force.
That force may create mechanical vibration.
That vibration may propagate through air as sound.

The sequence is simple:

Electrical energy → electromagnetic force → mechanical vibration → sound

So when a machine makes sound, we are often hearing the physical consequence of invisible electrical and electromagnetic activity acting through real materials.

A transformer hum is not just a hum.
A coil whine is not just an annoyance.
A motor tone is not just background sound.

Each may carry information about load, switching, resonance, speed, stress, degradation, or operating condition.

In that sense, sound is not only noise.

It is evidence.

Modern engineering often tries to eliminate these sounds, and in many cases that is exactly the right goal. Quieter machines are usually better machines.

But before we dismiss the sound, we should understand it.

Because what we hear may be the system revealing its hidden state.

Machines do not speak with language.

They speak through the transformation of energy inside matter.

And sometimes that hidden physics reaches us through the oldest interface of all:

sound.

Perhaps machines have always been speaking.
We simply learned to call their language noise.

Fundamental is:

Electromagnetism shapes atoms, chemical bonds, materials, and most of the physical behavior we experience directly.
Human bodies, machines, wires, motors, coils, transformers, and circuits are all built from matter whose behavior is governed largely by electromagnetic interactions.
When electrical energy flows through these materials, it can become:
electromagnetic force,
mechanical motion,
vibration,
and then sound.

So the sound is not random.

It is one visible or audible form of energy transformation inside matter.

A good way to say it is:

Machines speak because the matter they are made of responds to electromagnetic energy. Sound is one of the natural signatures of that transformation.

The theory follows one deterministic physical chain instead of moving many examples and side topics:

Electromagnetism shapes matter → electrical energy acts on that matter → force is created → structures vibrate → vibration becomes sound → sound carries evidence.

That is a clear path of idea from beginning to end.

The real thesis is:

Machines speak because the matter they are made from responds physically to electromagnetic energy. Sound is one natural signature of that transformation.

Bottom line:​Machines Speak Through Matter​That title is simpler and connects directly to the argument. The ending is also excellent:

Perhaps machines have always been speaking.
We simply learned to call their language noise.
